Lessons.Title: Equations and Their Graphs
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning objective: understand graphs as sets of solution pairs, determine whether a plotted point satisfies a linear equation, graph it using technology or a labelled manual alternative, and interpret axes in context. Edulytiks first-party source-aligned instruction for Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 2 Lesson 5, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/2/5/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). Building On 8.EE.B and 8.F.B.5; Addressing HSA-CED.A.2, HSA-CED.A.3, HSA-REI.D.10.

Original scenario: a community art club charges $6 registration and $4 per session, so total y=4x+6 dollars for number x≥0 of sessions (whole x). As a mathematical line over all real x the equation has infinitely many solutions; the meaningful scenario restricts x≥0 to integers. Graphing technology may draw the whole line, which should not be mistaken for permissible fractional attendance.

Data points (0,6),(1,10),(2,14),(3,18) lie on the equation. Pair (2,16) does not because 4×2+6=14, and (−1,2) satisfies the algebraic line but is not admissible in the modeled setting. Explain both the algebraic and contextual distinctions.

Student task: sketch or graph electronically the line and the feasible whole-number model, test candidate points, exchange a context with a peer and explain what an off-graph point would claim. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, max 8): correctly labelled graph, correct substitution checks, context and domain explanation, correct technology disclosure (real graphing versus manual drawing).

KeyConcepts.Title: Graph as solution set
KeyConcepts.Definition: Every point on the graph satisfies the equation.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Substitute x and y from a point.

KeyConcepts.Title: Slope and intercept
KeyConcepts.Definition: The y-intercept is value at x=0 and slope is change in y per unit change in x.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use coefficients and verify a second point.
KeyConcepts.Example: The line has intercept 6 and slope 4.

KeyConcepts.Title: Context-limited graph
KeyConcepts.Definition: A real-life situation may admit fewer values than the full real line.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Impose the whole-number and nonnegative domains.

WorkedExamples.Title: Generate accurate point table
WorkedExamples.Question: For y=4x+6, find y at x=0,1,2,3.
WorkedExamples.Method: Explain the equivalence or contextual calculation and verify substitutions independently.
Steps: Every one-unit increase in x raises y by four.

WorkedExamples.Title: Test an off-graph pair
WorkedExamples.Question: Is (2,16) on y=4x+6?
WorkedExamples.Method: Explain the equivalence or contextual calculation and verify substitutions independently.
Steps: At two sessions the genuine club total is $14.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No, (2,16) is not on the line.

WorkedExamples.Title: Separate algebraic and contextual solutions
WorkedExamples.Question: Does (−1,2) satisfy the line, and is it a valid purchase?
WorkedExamples.Method: Explain the equivalence or contextual calculation and verify substitutions independently.
Steps: The pair satisfies the full linear equation.
Negative sessions do not describe an admissible attendance choice.
The context's solution set is a discrete subset of the real graph.
WorkedExamples.Check: x must be a nonnegative integer.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Calling any point in the coordinate plane a solution
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Only points satisfying the relation lie on its graph.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming every point on a drawn real line is a physical option
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Real-valued graphing software ignores discrete context constraints unless specified.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Explain and mark only admissible session counts.

SummaryPoints: The graph contains all solution pairs to a two-variable equation.
y=4x+6 has slope 4, intercept 6 and point (2,14).
A contextual domain may be discrete even if a graphing tool draws a continuous line.
Teacher evaluates the graph, units and explanation; technology use cannot be inferred from text.
